A Guide to Starting a Start-Up

Who, What, When, Where, Why.

A vast majority of all questioned can be summarized into these 5 words. These are words that, as children ( and sometimes even now ) we use to bug our parents about every curiosity we had, no matter how big or small. These are also the questions you need to ask yourself when contemplating starting up your own online business or application.

Please keep in mind that this is by no means an official "Be all. End all" solution or guide to a web based start up, these are simply points that I've observed while building for the web

For now, we're just going to touch on the first question; WHO, I'll edit this post later, when I have a bit more time to do so.

 

Who

Who is probably the most important question that you need to ask yourself in your pursuit of fame and glory on the web. Why is it more important than the other questions? Because "WHO" dictates your audience, which in turn dictates HOW you're going to tackle your idea and WHY you're pursuing it in the first place. Your target audience could be anything; teenagers, old men, middle aged women, athletes, businessmen, painters, construction workers, photographers. Knowing WHO you're building your start up for is the most crucial part of the process. If you don't know your audience, then you don't know what specifics you'll need to include in your application or website.

 

For example:

An application for photographers may be something as simple as a platform for hosting images, or as complex as a set of image editing tools to change the contrast or other properties in a picture. There are tons of image hosting sites out there, so that probably isn't something that's going to be worth your time or effort. A solid, image manipulation website with advanced features and sharing options, that's something that's a bit harder to come by, and most of the pre-existing ones aren't that powerful.

Likewise, an application or website directed at a contractor needs something entirely different. Is it an e-commerce solution to buy tools and materials from? Is it going to be a comprehensive, easy-to-read and access directory of safety protocols and guidelines that a worker can quickly access with their mobile device? Or maybe it's a portfolio site, where contractors from around the world can upload pictures of their crowning achievements so that locals in their area can see what kind of work they can do, and decide who they want to remodel their home?

If you're targeting teenagers, most of the time you can win them over with beautiful user interfaces and flashy graphics. Whereas if your audience was an older generation, they may need to easily access information with something a bit more simplistic.

I know this is sort of delving into the realms of the WHAT, but all these questions blend together at some point and quite frequently cross over.

 

What

 

Our next question delves into the core of your platform. What the hell is it even going to be?

You've figured out who your target audience is, but what sort of platform do you want to provide them that doesn't already exist? Social networks like Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Vine, etc. take care of social networking for almost every age group and even if there is a unique niche, a quick google search will probably find a networking site for some group of people. But if not, you may have found your platform.

Staying on topic with our online photo editing studio (let's call it photowesome because I'm tired and can't come up with a better name) , it is a platform that has been attempted many times, but never quite perfected. Most people would rather download photo editing software such as Photoshop and do their professional edits there. But what is there was an online solution that was equally as powerful as photoshop, a tenth of the price, and multitudes faster? Now you have a platform that you can sell.

So we have our platform, Photowesome. We already have some huge selling points; Cheaper, Faster, but with the same power as Photoshop. Now you need to build it.

 

When

  This one is a relatively short question, when can you get it done by? If the technology is there, and modern browsers are being run on capable computers with a steady internet connection, how fast can you build this application? If you've thought of an idea, have no doubt that someone else has though of it, do they have the resources available to make it happen? Who knows. What you have to worry about is getting things moving. There is no time like the present to kickstart an idea that could very well be your livelyhood for years to come.

When can I get started. When can I get financial backing for my project When should I get a business licence When is my dad coming home from the corner store after getting smokes, IT'S BEEN TEN YEARS YOU UNGRATEFUL ASSHOLE. clears throat Apologies...

 

Where

 

Where, oh where has the time gone?

"Where" isn't a question that I can answer for you, but it's something that could impact your business in lots of ways, most of them financial.

Where are you going to host your platform? Naturally, to start you don't need much. A small server from Digital Ocean will probably get you started in the right direction, and it's only $4.99 a month to get their smallest tier server up and running. (If you sign up with the link, you'll get a $10 credit, that's two free months of server hosting). Next, I'd heavily recommend CloudFlare. CloudFlare not only acts as your DNS host, but also caches your website more efficiently and should your server go down, it will serve you the latest backup copy of your site. (Do not activate this feature if you're in development, you'll run into all sorts of frustrating problems).

Where, if it gets to that point, is your business going to be based? Do you have a P.O box somewhere, a physical building your renting, or are you just going to base it out of your mother's basement? There are lots of states ( and provinces ) that have funding benefits and tax breaks for people starting up a tech business. It's up to you where you go, but it's definitely worth looking into.

 

Why

 

Finally, why are you even doing this? It sounds like a whole lot of work just to make a platform that MAYBE people will use. And yeah, you would be right, there is a lot of work involved in this, but the the potential payoff from filling in a niche that a lot of people are wanting and potentially raking in a lot of money is far more rewarding than having a 9-5 desk job at some company that doesn't appreciate your talents.

Maybe this isn't for you, maybe your better suited to be an employee than an entrepreneur, but you'll never know unless you try. Let's go back to the question: Why?

I can think of lots of reasons why.

You work your own hours You pay your own wages You (potentially) have employees instead of BEING an employee Your platform could give you a very nice life if you price it right That ever present thought in the back of your mind that Google or Microsoft might one day pick up your platform / software. Eternal bragging rights of saying "Hey, you know Platform X, yeah, I built that shit. That's awesome.

 

Again, these are just a few of the many questions you need to ask yourself ( and others ) when considering doing a web start up. This is by no means a definitive guide and is probably missing a whole whack load of information, but It's written from (addmitedly failed) experiences and I hope from reading some or all of this information, it's given you a bit of insight into the world of web start-ups.

 

Note: My start ups failed because I had partners bail on me, time restrictions and other more pressing commitments

I'm typing this as I wear my Gunnar Rockets. My friend won them at a hack-a-thon at our University and gave them to me. I was a competitive FPS player at that point so I acquired them for that purpose.

For gaming: They actually work great - in terms of reducing eye-strain and boosting screen contrast so targets are easier to spot. Plus they let you get into that l33t MLG quicksc0pe mindset while you're playing.

For computer use: This was actually a secondary priority for me, but I'd say I actually use them at work more than anything else now. I write and edit video, so I too stare at a screen endlessly and often need to be pretty focused. On top of that I get mindnumbingly awful migraines from time to time and my eyes can sometimes get quite sore (that awful throbbing pain behind your eyes) when I look at a screen for too long. These work wonders for reducing the level of strain I experience. I wouldn't say it's a complete elimination, but it's definitely significant - to the extent that you can feel the difference. If I had to quantify it (pretty useless because it's a subjective 'feeling') I'd say it's reduced by about 50-75%.

So yes, they do actually work pretty well in terms of their functional uses. On top of that they're really sturdy. I frequently stuff them in a packed bag with a ton of heavy stuff and they are still in pristine condition.

I got these glasses for nearly free, but if I were to ever lose them I would immediately purchase a new pair at full price.
